styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small chair seen from the back. Its outline is a tinted dark brown (0% near-neutral dark edge pixels), so it does not have the near-black sticker look. It has only 8 distinct colours against 14 on the comparable bench reference, and I read about 3 shading steps on the wood against 5-6 on Beodeul wood. The back and seat look like mostly one mid-brown with a dark edge and a few highlight pixels, and I see no grain or per-plank shading like the bench's. The per-tile and flat-coverage facts are uninformative because the piece is smaller than one tile, so I judged density by eye. By eye it is thinner and flatter than the bench, and a careful artist would likely see it as less developed next to the references. When in doubt, fail.

surfaces.part: backrest panel seen from behind, with a light top edge on row 3

answer.evidence: The silhouette is a 10px-wide panel (rows 2-12) on two narrow 6px legs (rows 13-15). The column scan shows a light edge on row 3, then a uniform brown face on rows 4-10, a dark base line on row 11 and legs below. This is the chair seen from behind, so the backrest hides the seat. No seat surface is visible: there is no ellipse, no band ending in an edge line with eave shadow, and no contents. The width profile has no seat-sized horizontal band. The backrest is exempt as seat_back, but the seat itself shows no top, so this reads as front_elevation, like the 'seat: band 2' reference.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small chair seen from behind, with only 8 distinct colours in total. The closest reference, the wood bench, has 14, and the other props have 11 to 40. The chair shows about 3 tones: a dark frame, a mid wood and a lighter back panel. The references carry about 5-6 steps, with per-plank highlights and grain. The back panel and seat read as flat fills with no grain dots or highlight and shadow pairs. The outline is a dark, mostly uniform line around the whole shape. Its tint is hard to read at this size, so I call it mixed, and it leans toward the sticker look rather than the selective dark-material outlines the references use. The per-tile facts are 0 for the candidate and for the bench and lamp, so they can't settle density. Judged by eye, the chair is clearly thinner and flatter than the bench and the other props. Given the shallow ramp, the flat panels and the doubtful outline, it would not sit comfortably beside the references, so it fails.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny chair or sign-like prop on the right of the magenta bar, and it is smaller than one 16x16 tile. The facts give 0 visible tones per tile, so I judged by eye. It uses only 8 distinct colours in total, against 11-40 for the references. It reads as a dark outline with one or two flat fills for wood and seat, so about 2 shading steps. The references have 4-6 steps: the bench has slat highlights, the hedge has leaf clumps, the well has stone-by-stone shading. The outline looks like a uniform dark line around the whole shape, which is the sticker look, rather than a dark tone of the adjacent wood. There is no grain, no highlight dots and no texture on the wood. Even next to the simple bench reference (14 colours, with per-slat shading), it looks thinner, flatter and more sticker-like. A careful artist would not accept it next to the references.
